name: Bath

attributes.attribute: British mythological site with healing hot springs
Celtic goddess of the site, merged with Minerva
site of the Celtic coin-throwing custom
source of 16,000 coins and more than 50 cursing tablets

sources: Ross, Anne, and Michael Cyprien. A Traveller’s Guide to Celtic Britain. Harrisburg, Pa.: Historical Times, 1985, 19.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text:
Bath is a British mythological site. It lies in the southwest of England. Great hot springs bubble from the earth there. The waters have been prized for healing for at least two thousand years. Some think the spring was used before the Celts. The records that survive date from Celtic times. The Romans named the town Aquae Sulis.

The Celts linked the site to their goddess Sul. The Romans folded Sul into their goddess Minerva. They built colonnaded temples and interior bathing rooms. These buildings stand today.

Celtic custom showed itself at Bath. People threw coins into the water. They also wrote curses on sheets of lead. Excavators have found 16,000 coins at the site. They have found more than 50 cursing tablets as well.

okr.objective: Describe Bath as a British healing site centered on the goddess Sul.
key_results: The Bath hot springs have healed for at least two thousand years.
The Roman called the site Aquae Sulis and merged Sul with Minerva.
Celtic custom at Bath included throwing coins and writing curses on lead.
Excavators found 16,000 coins and more than 50 cursing tablets.
